report.tagline: A government-backed open network that lets any shopping app show products from any seller app, like UPI did for payments.
report.simpleSummary: On Amazon or Swiggy, the buyer, the seller and the delivery all live inside one company's app. ONDC breaks that up. A shop can list once on any seller app, and buyers can find it from any buyer app, like Paytm, Magicpin or Ola. ONDC is not an app itself. It is a set of shared rules so these apps can talk to each other, the way UPI lets PhonePe send money to a Google Pay user. The idea is lower fees for sellers and more choice for buyers.

overview.whatItDoes: ONDC (Open Network for Digital Commerce) is a non-profit set up by the Indian government in 2021. It writes open rules (protocols) that let buyer apps, seller apps and delivery companies connect. Any approved app can join. It covers groceries, food, fashion, rides, metro tickets, logistics and financial services.
howItWorks: A buyer app (Paytm, Magicpin, Ola, Mystore, PhonePe for some services) shows products from all sellers on the network.
A seller app (like Mystore, eSamudaay or a POS company) helps shops list products and take orders.
Logistics partners (Loadshare, Shadowfax and others) pick up and deliver orders from any seller.
ONDC sits in the middle: it keeps a registry of participants and rules for search, order, payment and disputes, but does not hold stock or money.
Sellers pay a much lower commission (about 8 to 10% across apps) versus 25 to 30% on big marketplaces.
Early growth was pushed by incentives paid to buyer apps, which were cut sharply in late 2024.
overview.valueProposition: For sellers: reach buyers on many apps without paying high marketplace fees or being locked into one platform. For buyers: more choice and sometimes lower prices. For India: a level field where no single company controls online commerce.

painPoints.pain: Big marketplaces charge sellers 25 to 40% commission.
painPoints.howSolved: Open network with about 8 to 10% fees and near-zero network fee.

painPoints.pain: Sellers are locked into one platform and its rules.
painPoints.howSolved: List once, appear on many buyer apps.

painPoints.pain: Drivers pay high commission on ride apps.
painPoints.howSolved: Mobility on ONDC (like Namma Yatri) uses low or subscription fees for drivers.

painPoints.pain: Small towns are poorly served by big platforms.
painPoints.howSolved: 70% of traffic comes from tier-2 and tier-3 cities; local sellers can join cheaply.

painPoints.pain: A few companies control data and rules of e-commerce.
painPoints.howSolved: Open protocols and a neutral network run by a non-profit.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Shared technical rules for search, order, pay, track and return.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Lets any app talk to any other app, which is the whole idea.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Lists approved buyer apps, seller apps and logistics partners.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Builds trust that every participant follows the rules.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Any seller can book delivery from any logistics partner on the network.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Small sellers get delivery without their own fleet.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: A shared process to raise and fix complaints across apps.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Without one company in charge, this is the weakest link for buyers.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Ride booking and metro and bus tickets through many apps.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Now the biggest share of volume, with 3 lakh+ daily transit tickets.

businessModel.summary: ONDC is a non-profit. It aims to cover its costs from small network fees on transactions, but these fees were postponed for most categories and only started in financial services. It has relied on funding from government-linked banks and institutions.

revenueStreams.detail: A small fee per transaction, planned from December 2024 but postponed for retail. Applies in financial services.
Fees for joining and certification of apps.
Backed by institutions like SIDBI, NABARD, Bank of Baroda and others.

businessModel.pricing: Network fee near zero for most retail. Seller apps and buyer apps set their own commissions; total for sellers is typically about 8 to 10%.
costDrivers: Incentives paid to apps to grow orders (cut from ₹2.5 crore to ₹30 lakh per app in late 2024)
businessModel.unitEconomics: ONDC itself earns almost nothing per order. On a ₹300 food order, the seller might pay 8 to 10% (₹24 to ₹30) split between buyer app, seller app and delivery. Delivery alone can cost ₹40 to ₹50. So someone, usually the buyer, pays a delivery fee, or the apps lose money. When ONDC paid incentives, it covered the gap. After incentives were cut, retail orders fell from 6.5 million in October 2024 to 4.6 million in February 2025. ONDC lost ₹147 crore in FY25 on ₹33 crore revenue. Per-order split is an estimate.

howTheyGetUsers: Big buyer apps like Paytm, Magicpin and Ola add ONDC sections
Incentives and discounts paid to apps to drive orders
Mobility apps like Namma Yatri attract drivers with low fees
Government push to MSMEs, farmer groups and transit systems
whatBringsUsersBack: Lower prices (when apps pass on savings)
Local shops not found on big apps
growth.moat: ONDC's edge is that it is neutral and government-backed, so any company can join without fearing a rival owns the rules. But a network is only strong if buyers and sellers both show up. Big platforms already have both, plus fast delivery and good support.

competitors.name: Amazon and Flipkart
competitors.positioning: Closed marketplaces with about 83% of e-commerce.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: ONDC is open and cheaper for sellers but lacks one company that owns the full experience and fixes problems.

competitors.name: Swiggy and Zomato
competitors.positioning: Food and quick commerce leaders with their own delivery fleets.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: ONDC food can be cheaper, but delivery speed and support are weaker.

competitors.name: Blinkit, Zepto, Instamart
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Quick commerce solved the speed problem; ONDC grocery cannot match it yet.

competitors.name: Uber and Rapido
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: ONDC mobility apps charge drivers less, which is why mobility grew fastest.

northStar.metric: Successful orders per month across the network (delivered without complaint)
northStar.why: ONDC only works if real orders reach buyers well. Counting successful, complaint-free orders shows both scale and quality, not just clicks or listings.

strengths: Much lower fees for sellers and drivers
Fast growth in mobility and transit
Reach in 1,000 cities and strong tier-2 and tier-3 use
weaknesses: Retail orders fell after incentives were cut
Clunky experience: more than half of surveyed users found it hard to use
No single owner for customer support and refunds
Has not started charging most network fees, so it depends on funding

improvementIdeas.idea: One-stop complaint desk with fixed refund timelines
improvementIdeas.problem: Buyers do not know who to complain to.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: Faster fixes, more trust, more repeat orders.

improvementIdeas.idea: Quality badge for seller apps and sellers
improvementIdeas.problem: Experience varies a lot across apps.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: Buyer apps show top-rated sellers first, lowering cancellations.

improvementIdeas.idea: Focus on categories where open wins (mobility, transit, local services)
improvementIdeas.problem: Retail and food compete with strong, fast incumbents.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: Grow where low fees clearly help.

improvementIdeas.idea: Small, clear network fee with seller savings shown
improvementIdeas.metricToTrack: Network fee revenue and seller churn

improvementIdeas.idea: Shared delivery hubs in tier-2 cities
improvementIdeas.problem: Delivery costs and speed hurt retail.

pmLessons: An open network needs a great experience on top. Lower fees alone do not beat fast, reliable apps.
Subsidies can create fake growth. When incentives stopped, retail orders dropped.
The UPI comparison has limits: payments are one simple action, but shopping has stock, delivery, returns and support.
Pick the use cases where your model clearly wins. ONDC found that in rides and transit, not in food.

interviewQuestions.question: Why did UPI succeed but ONDC struggle in retail?
interviewQuestions.hint: Compare complexity (one action vs many steps), pain point (cash vs already-good apps), time with zero fees (8 years vs 2), and who owns support.

interviewQuestions.question: What should ONDC's north star metric be?
interviewQuestions.hint: Successful, complaint-free orders per month. Explain why GMV or seller count alone can mislead.

interviewQuestions.question: You are PM at Paytm. Should you keep ONDC in your app?
interviewQuestions.hint: Look at orders, margin per order, support costs and brand risk. Consider keeping only categories that perform.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you fix buyer trust on ONDC?
interviewQuestions.hint: Map the complaint journey across buyer app, seller app and logistics. Suggest a single desk, refund SLAs and seller ratings.

interviewQuestions.question: Why did mobility grow faster than food on ONDC?
interviewQuestions.hint: Rides are simple, drivers gain a lot from low fees, and quality is easy to judge. Food needs stock, packing and delivery coordination.

glossary.meaning: A system where any approved company can connect using shared rules, instead of one company controlling it.

The share of each sale a platform keeps as its fee.

Gross merchandise value: the total value of goods sold through a platform.
Grocery delivery in 10 to 30 minutes from small local warehouses called dark stores.
The one number that best shows a product gives real value to users.
Something that makes it hard for competitors to copy you or take your users.
A number you watch to make sure a change does not cause harm elsewhere.
Service level agreement: a promised time or standard, like refunds within 3 days.
How much money is made or lost on one order or one customer.
